In our experiment, we manipulated meta-ecosystems consisting of autotrophic and heterotrophic patches, varying the relative size of these patches (referred to as meta-ecosystem types AD, ED, and HD) and their connectivity (unconnected versus connected). Now, we want to know whether, at the local ecosystem level, the connectivity of the ecosystem interacted with ecosystem size to affect this specific response variable. Essentially, we are interested in understanding if ecosystem size modulated the impact of spatial feedback locally. To begin, we plot how this response variable varied across different treatments throughout the experiment, represented by mean values with a 95% confidence interval.

```{r}
plot.ecosystems.points(ds_ecosystems,
                       ecosystem_size_and_trophy_selected,
                       connections_selected,
                       response_variable,
                       legend_row_n_input = 3)
```

```{r}
                                      ecosystem_size_and_trophy_selected,

```


 <br>

Following this initial inspection, we proceed to analyse differences among ecosystems. Our first step involves filtering the data to isolate the relevant data for analysis. Specifically, we exclude data points where the response variable couldn't be computed, as well as time points preceding the initial disturbance and resource flow. Then we plot the data to make sure that what filtered the data in the right way.

```{r}
filtered_data = ds_ecosystems %>%
  filter(ecosystem_size_and_trophy %in% ecosystem_size_and_trophy_selected,
         time_point >= first_time_point_model,
         time_point <= last_time_point_model,!is.na(!!sym(response_variable))) %>%
  mutate(ecosystem_ID = as.character(ecosystem_ID),
         size = NA,
         size = case_when(ecosystem_size == "Small" ~ "S",
                          ecosystem_size == "Medium" ~ "M",
                          ecosystem_size == "Large" ~ "L",
                          TRUE ~ size),
         size = factor(size, levels = c("S", "M", "L")))
```

```{r}
plot.ecosystems.points(filtered_data,
                       ecosystem_size_and_trophy_selected,
                       connections_selected,
                       response_variable,
                       legend_row_n_input = 3)
```

 <br>

Then, we develop a mixed effect model (`model`) with lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) to examine how the interaction between ecosystem size and connectivity influences the response variable, treating ecosystem ID and time as random effects (**Response variable \~ size \* connection + (1 \| ecosystem_ID) + (1 \| day)**, see [this link](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lme4/vignettes/lmer.pdf) for how to code). In this model we don't use a Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) because, while REML is robust to missing data, it may not perform well with very small sample sizes, especially when the number of random effects is large relative to the number of observations (ChatGPT). After having created the model, we show its summary and plot its residuals. The summary of the model allows us to look at the random effects, as well as differences among levels calculated using a t-test that employs Satterthwaite's method to estimate the degrees of freedom for the two groups. This method is conservative in order to prevent false positives (Li & Redden, 2015). An alternative method that could be used is the Kenward-Roger's method, however, it is expected to perform similarly. Because the model utilises Satterthwaite's method, it should entail a Welch t-test (according to information gleaned from [this Wikipedia page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welch%E2%80%93Satterthwaite_equation)), which does not assume equal variance in the two groups. There is no option in this package to alter the type of t-test. These p-values are calculated by examining whether the slope of the response variable against the predictor variable differs significantly from zero.

```{r}

## - Create mixed effect model - ##

# In the ouput lmerModLmerTest which means that it's a Linear Mixed Model from the lmerTest package

model = lmer(
   get(response_variable) ~
     size * connection +
     (1 | ecosystem_ID) +
     (1 | day),
   data = filtered_data,
   REML = FALSE,
   control = lmerControl(optimizer = "Nelder_Mead"))
```

```{r}

## - Show summary of the model -- ##

print(summary(model), digits = 3)
```

```{r child = here("r_files", "check_random_effects.Rmd"), eval = (trophy_selected == "autotrophic")}
```

```{r}

## - Plot residuals of the model -- ##

qqnorm(resid(model))

create.res.vs.fit.ecosystems(model,
                             filtered_data)
```

 <br>

However, this model's output complicates understanding the fixed effects. To enhance clarity in demonstrating the statistical significance of fixed effects, we employ a type III ANOVA on the full model. This method accommodates unbalanced designs and yields the same results to type I ANOVA in balanced designs ([Uni Goettingen](https://md.psych.bio.uni-goettingen.de/mv/unit/lm_cat/lm_cat_unbal_ss_explained.html)). We utilise Satterthwaite's method to estimate the degrees of freedom for the two groups. But just knowing whether or not there is an effect is not enough. If there is an effect, we want to know which levels were different. Therefore, we proceed to analyse the contrasts among levels, ensuring that the P values go through a Tukey adjustment to account for the multiple comparisons (see [this link for contrast coding](https://aosmith.rbind.io/2019/04/15/custom-contrasts-emmeans/)).

```{r}

## - Perform Type III ANOVA on the model - ##

anova_output = anova(model)
anova_output
```

<details>

<summary>Click to view how the contrasts were coded</summary>

```{r}

## - Analyse the contrasts among levels -- ##

emmeans_output = emmeans(model,
                         specs = pairwise ~ size:connection,
                         adjust = "tukey",
                         bias.adj = TRUE,
                         lmer.df = "satterthwaite")
emmeans_output

S_unconnected = c(1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)
M_unconnected = c(0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0)
L_unconnected = c(0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0)
S_connected = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0)
M_connected = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0)
L_connected = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1)
```

</details>

```{r}
n_of_digits = 3
contrasts = contrast(emmeans_output, 
         method = list("Small connection effect" = S_connected - S_unconnected,
                       "Medium connection effect" = M_connected - M_unconnected,
                       "Large connection effect" = L_connected - L_unconnected,
                       "Size effect (L vs S)" = L_unconnected - S_unconnected,
                       "Size effect (M vs S)" = M_unconnected - S_unconnected)) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  mutate(p.value = round(p.value, digits = n_of_digits),
         estimate = round(estimate, digits = n_of_digits),
         SE = round(SE, digits = n_of_digits),
         df = round(df, digits = n_of_digits),
         t.ratio = round(t.ratio, digits = n_of_digits),
         e = "",
         e = ifelse(p.value > 0.1, 
                           "",
                           e),
         e = ifelse(p.value < 0.05, 
                           "*",
                           e),
         e = ifelse(p.value < 0.01, 
                           "**",
                           e),
         e = ifelse(p.value < 0.001, 
                           "***",
                           e)) %>%
  rename(" " = e)

contrasts
```

 <br>

```{r}

S_connection_estimate = S_connection_contrast$estimate %>% round(., digits = digits_estimate) %>% as.character()
```
